Definition: At a branch value local sheet labels coalesce, so the regular ij-trajectory ODE is restricted to the complement of the branch locus and local branch/junction rules are stated separately.
Definition: Closed webs lift to absolute one-cycles; defect-ended open webs have the explicitly stated relative-homology boundary z^(j)-z^(i) or z_2^(j)-z_1^(i).

The Definition explicitly assumes ACω for the imported mathematical trace chain. The compact self-adjoint spectral theorem uses the countable-union result and finite-eigenspace basis selection, and the singular-value decomposition also uses countable basis selection. The positive-square-root proof uses ACω through norm-limit compactness and the complete-and-totally-bounded compactness theorem. This is a mathematical premise, not a physical assumption, and no choice is made to construct the model-supplied sectors.

citations.quote:
For distinct sheets $i,j$, a regular **$ij$-trajectory of Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (WKB) phase** $\vartheta_{\rm W}\in\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ is a $C^1$ immersed path $z:I\to C\setminus\operatorname{Branch}(\pi)$, for an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, with $\dot z\ne0$ and

$$\operatorname{Im}\!\left(e^{-i\vartheta_{\rm W}}(\lambda^{(i)}-\lambda^{(j)})(\dot z)\right)=0.$$

A geometric WKB network is generated from the maximal such trajectories issuing from branch points and from the local junction rule: when compatible $ij$- and $jk$-trajectories meet, an $ik$-trajectory may issue from their joint.

A **finite web** is a finite connected metric ribbon graph: each edge has positive finite length and a cyclic order at each vertex; each internal vertex is trivalent and maps to a network joint, and each external univalent vertex maps to a branch point.

The physical charge group $\Gamma_{\mathcal T}$ is a model-specified quotient of a subgroup $\Gamma_0\le\Gamma_{\rm geom}$, supplied with a surjective quotient map $\rho:\Gamma_0\to\Gamma_{\mathcal T}$; it is not identified with all of $H_1(\widetilde\Sigma;\mathbb Z)$ by notation alone.

derivations.claim: On the affine curve $y^3=x(x-1)$, $dx/y^2$ cubes to the specified differential. There are exactly three fully ramified points, over $0,1,\infty$. Near the first two, use $y$ as a coordinate: differentiation gives $dx/y^2=3\,dy/(2x-1)$, which extends holomorphically and is nonzero. Near infinity take a parameter $t$ with $x=t^{-3}$ and $y=t^{-2}h(t)$, where $h(t)^3=1-t^3$ and $h(0)=1$; then $dx/y^2=-3h(t)^{-2}dt$, again holomorphic and nonzero. Away from these points the cover is unramified and the form is nonzero. Along the lift $q$ of $[0,1]$ with $y=-[x(1-x)]^{1/3}$ the form is positive real, and $\int_q\lambda_{\rm geom}=\beta$. The integral converges because both endpoint exponents are $-2/3>-1$. The three oriented lifts are $q,\tau q,\tau^2q$, and their integrals are $\beta,\omega\beta,\omega^2\beta$.

The inverse image $G=\pi^{-1}([0,1])$ is a graph with two vertices and these three edges. Its complement is one open disk: $\mathbb P^1\setminus[0,1]$ is an open disk containing the single remaining branch value $\infty$, and its punctured-disk cover is connected with cyclic monodromy of order three; cutting along a radius gives three slit disks glued cyclically, whose missing central point fills to one disk by the local degree-three model. Thus the compact surface has a cell decomposition with $G$ as its one-skeleton and one two-cell. The oriented attaching boundary traverses each graph edge once in each direction, so its cellular boundary is zero. The integral cycle group of $G$ consists of the triples $(n_0,n_1,n_2)$ with $n_0+n_1+n_2=0$; a basis is $(1,-1,0),(0,1,-1)$. Consequently $[q-\tau q]$ and $[\tau q-\tau^2q]$ form a basis of $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Z)$, and the full period group is $a(\mathbb Z+\omega\mathbb Z)$, with $a=(1-\omega)\beta$. Integration is unchanged by homotopy or a boundary: subdivide a homotopy or singular two-simplex into finitely many pieces contained in primitive disks, then the primitive endpoint differences cancel on internal edges. This also justifies using the cellular cycle representatives to compute all periods.

Define $f:\Sigma\to\mathbb C/(a\mathbb Z+a\omega\mathbb Z)$ by integration from $\widetilde A$ modulo the period group. Step 2.1 makes this well-defined, and its derivative is the nowhere-zero form from step 1.1, so it is a local biholomorphism. Compactness makes its image closed; local invertibility makes it open, so connectedness of the target makes it surjective and a finite covering. The two loops in step 2.1 map to the two target lattice generators; hence the induced fundamental-group image is the entire target group $\mathbb Z^2$. A connected covering with this image has one sheet: lifting target loops permutes its fiber transitively, whereas loops in the image fix the chosen point, so surjectivity leaves only that point. Thus $f$ is a biholomorphism. Dividing its coordinate by $a$ gives the asserted $w$ and $\lambda_{\rm geom}=a\,dw$. Along $q$, $w$ runs straight from $0$ to $\beta/a=1/(1-\omega)=(2+\omega)/3$, so constant flat-speed parametrization is exactly $p(t)=[t(2+\omega)/3]$. Integration also gives $w(\tau P)=\omega w(P)$. The fixed classes of this rotation solve $(1-\omega)w\in\mathbb Z+\omega\mathbb Z$; the determinant of multiplication by $1-\omega$ is $3$, and the three distinct solutions are the displayed $\widetilde A,\widetilde B,\widetilde C$. The remaining branch point therefore has the asserted coordinate $\widetilde C$.

The displacement $(2+\omega)/3=1/2+i\sqrt3/6$ has unit-coordinate length $1/\sqrt3$ and coordinate angle $\vartheta_w=\pi/6$. Since $a=(1-\omega)\beta=\sqrt3\beta e^{-i\pi/6}$, its actual flat length is $|a|/\sqrt3=\beta$ and its actual geometric phase is $\vartheta_{\rm KT}=0$. The ordered sheet difference $(1-\omega)\lambda_{\rm geom}$ along this path has phase $\vartheta_{\rm W}=-\pi/6$, with positive real part after multiplication by $e^{i\pi/6}$. The coordinate-slope formula has coprime $(p_0,q_0)=(2,1)$ and determinant $4-2+1=3$; the rotation from $w$ to the flat coordinate must be included when interpreting this as a network phase. Finally, $\int_p\lambda_{\rm geom}=a(2+\omega)/3=\beta$.

A point on the open segment has basis coordinates $(2s/3,s/3)$ for $0<s<1$. It cannot equal a lattice translate of $\widetilde A$, since that would require an integer second coordinate $s/3\in(0,1/3)$; it cannot equal a translate of $\widetilde B$, since the second coordinate would require $s=1+3n$ for an integer $n$, which has no solution in $(0,1)$; and it cannot equal a translate of $\widetilde C$, since it would require $s=2+3n$, also with no solution in $(0,1)$. Thus the open segment contains no branch point. It is embedded on the torus since a nonzero difference between two points on it has norm less than $1/\sqrt3$, whereas every nonzero lattice vector has norm at least $1$. Its projection under $\pi$ also has no interior self-identification: for $0<s,t<1$, the basis coordinates of $p(t)-\tau(p(s))$ are $((2t+s)/3,(t-s)/3)$, which cannot both be integers, and those of $p(t)-\tau^2(p(s))$ are $((2t+s)/3,(t+2s)/3)\in(0,1)^2$, also not a lattice vector. Therefore the projected path is an embedded regular trajectory from one conical branch value to the other. The WKB network contains this trajectory from each endpoint, in both orientations; the two orientations form a double wall.

The graph $T=[0,1]$ with its single edge assigned length $\beta$ in the KT cover metric is finite and connected, has two univalent external vertices and no internal vertices, and maps isometrically to the projected double wall because $\pi$ is an unramified local isometry on its open edge. In the GMN sheet-difference metric its edge length is $|1-\omega|\beta=\sqrt3\,\beta=c$, whose GMN-normalized value is $c/\pi$ in the source's geometric units; no physical mass is asserted. Thus it satisfies the finite-web definition in either explicitly declared convention.

The deck rotation $\tau$ fixes the two endpoints, so $p-\tau(p)$ is the explicit cycle of [F4]. Its period is $\int_{p-\tau(p)}\lambda_{\rm geom}=(1-\omega)\int_p\lambda_{\rm geom}=(1-\omega)\beta=a=ce^{-i\pi/6}\ne0$. In the unit-lattice coordinate the displacement of this cycle is $(1-\omega)(2+\omega)/3=1$, agreeing with this period. It is a primitive nonzero homology class by the basis computation in step 2.1; independently, its nonzero period excludes a boundary by the primitive-disk argument there. Its phase $-\pi/6$ is congruent to $\vartheta_{\rm KT}+\pi/2=\pi/2$ modulo $\pi/3$; this congruence is only a phase check and does not identify the explicit cycle with a canonical lift. This proves the nonzero geometric class and exact period, not an unconditional physical identification.

Under the assumptions of [A1], the descended physical central charge is $Z_{\mathcal T}(\rho(\gamma_{\rm geom}))=\pi^{-1}\int_{\gamma_{\rm geom}}m_*\lambda_{\rm geom}=m_*a/\pi\ne0$. Since $Z_{\mathcal T}$ is additive, it sends zero to zero, so $\rho(\gamma_{\rm geom})\ne0$. Without the assumptions in [A1], no physical charge image follows.
